The Phase 4 Report also extended the study forecast horizon through 2050 in order to capture the impacts of achieving the State’s power-sector decarbonization goals under California Senate Bill (SB) 100 (De León, Chapter 312, Statutes of 2018), which requires that renewable energy and zero-carbon resources supply 100 percent of the State’s electric retail sales by 2045. The Phase 4 Report considered the potential of shed and shift DR resources, as obtained both through traditional supply-side (dispatchable) DR programs and through dynamic electricity prices that facilitate shape DR. As it can be difficult to quantify and communicate the impacts of shape DR in units that are comparable to event-based DR, the Phase 4 Report developed and utilized the metrics “effective shed” and “effective shift” (i.e., how much load reduction or load shifting (from shape DR) occurs at times when shed or shift events are likely to occur). These resources are referred to in the Phase 4 Report as “shape-as-shed” and “shape-as-shift.” The Phase 4 Report showed that dramatic growth is expected in the economic potential of DR resources in California through 2050, with load flexible end-uses characterized, according to the trends in their potential over the forecast period, as: steady workhorses;6 rising stars;7 emerging performers;8 declining resources;9 and development opportunities.10 The Phase 4 Report results also indicated that a business-as-usual (BAU) approach to customer enrollment underlay more than a fivefold gap between the economic and the BAU achievable resources for both shed and shift DR. The report noted that understanding how best to reduce the sizable barrier that customer enrollment and participation in DR programs present to realizing the full potential of cost-effective DR in California would go far in helping California to achieve its energy goals. In a similar vein, the Phase 4 Report showed that customer price response – under the assumptions of universal enrollment in a dynamic tariff that is conceptually akin to the California Flexible Unified Signal for Energy (CalFUSE) tariff structure (described in Table 1 and in the text below) – could capture some 40-50% of the technical potential for shed and shift DR in the form of shape DR; much of that would be available at zero cost through manual customer response. By 2025, those zero-cost resources would amount to some 7 GW of effective shed and 3.5 GWh of effective shift resource. 6 Steady workhorses are important sources of DR potential throughout the Phase 4 period of analysis. The most important of these are industrial process loads, agricultural pumping, and commercial and residential refrigeration. 7 Rising stars are new electrified loads that rapidly grow to be among the largest available DR resources. These are light-duty vehicle (LDV) electric vehicle charging (EVSE) at residential buildings, medium/heavy-duty vehicle EVSE, and residential water heating. 8 Emerging performers are new electrified or newly-connected loads that become increasingly important over the time period of analysis.
